name: Shadow-stick direction
summary: Two shadow tips fifteen minutes apart give you a west-east line anywhere on Earth, with no compass and no clock.

materials.item: a straight stick about a metre long

steps.text: Push the stick upright into level ground where its shadow falls clearly.
Mark the very TIP of the shadow with a pebble. That mark is WEST.
steps.why: The sun tracks westward across the sky, so the shadow tip tracks eastward — the first mark is always the western one, in either hemisphere.

steps.text: Wait 15-30 minutes — longer gives a longer, more accurate baseline.
Mark the new shadow tip. That mark is EAST.
The line joining the two marks runs west-east. Stand with the first mark under your left foot and the second under your right: you are facing NORTH.

verify: Cross-check with the sun's own arc: it rises in the eastern half of the sky and sets in the western half everywhere on Earth.
In the northern hemisphere the midday sun sits to the south; in the southern hemisphere, to the north. The result should agree.
limits: It gives DIRECTION, not position. Knowing which way is north does not tell you where you are or where help is.
Accuracy is roughly good enough to walk a straight line by — not good enough to navigate to a point.
It needs sun and reasonably level ground; on a steep slope the geometry distorts.
It is least accurate near the equinoxes at high latitude and around local noon, when the shadow moves fast and short.
cautions: Knowing north is only useful with a decision about where to go. In most lost-person cases, staying put and signalling is the better one.
